pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule; identify features NOT explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'generate and describe linear number sequences'; reasoning about pattern features.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.5 — 'generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms … and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate.'
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: GENERATE (apply a term-to-term rule accurately) and NOTICE-AND-EXPLAIN (spot an emergent feature — alternating odd/even, all even, a repeating units digit — and justify it from the rule's structure). The emphasis, as with times-table patterns, is on the informal EXPLANATION ('add 3 flips parity each time because 3 is odd'), moving from spotting to reasoning. Shape patterns (growing sequences) connect the term number to a count, seeding the position-to-term (nth-term) idea. Use a T-table (term number vs value) and concrete/pictorial growing patterns.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): generate terms from a rule and continue a shape pattern. Tier B (age 9–10): notice an emergent feature (alternating odd/even; always even) and describe it. Tier C (age 10): explain informally WHY the feature must continue, from the rule's structure.
bestPractices: Separate and then connect the two demands: generate accurately, THEN look for a feature the rule didn't state and explain it.
Press for informal explanation grounded in structure ('adding an odd number flips odd↔even'), not restatement of the observation.
Use a T-table (term number vs value) so emergent features and the position-to-value link become visible.
Include growing SHAPE patterns (dots/tiles) alongside number patterns, connecting the picture to the count and seeding nth-term thinking.
Encourage prediction ('what will the 10th term be? will it be odd or even?') and verification.
keyRepresentations: T-table (term number ↔ value) — exposing emergent features
Growing shape/dot pattern — term number as a count
Number line / hundred square — visualising step patterns and parity
Colour-coded terms (odd/even) to make features pop
commonMisconceptions: Applying the rule inconsistently or miscounting steps when generating terms.
'Explaining' a feature by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Assuming a short-run feature always holds without justification (over-generalising).
Confusing the term-to-term rule with a position-to-term rule.
Not distinguishing the starting number's role from the step's role in an emergent feature.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule, then notice a feature the rule did NOT state (alternating odd/even, all-even, a repeating units-digit cycle) and explain informally WHY it must continue from the rule's structure. The teaching goal is to move from spotting a feature to justifying it (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), using a term-number vs value table and growing shape pictures to seed position-to-term thinking.

activities.title: Generate, then colour by parity to spot a hidden feature
feedback: If the differences between your terms aren't all the same (e.g. 1, 4, 7, 9, 12), you added to the wrong term or changed the step partway — mark the +3 jump between every pair to enforce a constant step.

If, when asked what else you notice, you only repeat 'it goes up by 3', look specifically at the last digits (1, 4, 7, 0, 3, 6, 9, 2 …) or at the odd/even pattern — those are features the rule didn't tell you.
Check your 10th term by continuing the sequence; the colour pattern should let you predict its parity before you compute it.
activities.rationale: Separating accurate generation from feature-noticing, and using a term-number vs value table plus parity colouring, makes emergent features and the position-to-value link visible, as the standard requires.
sourceClaims: Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
learnerActions: Take the rule 'start at 1, add 3' and write the first eight terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.
Mark each 'add 3' jump between consecutive terms (on a number line or by an arrow) so the step stays constant.
Colour or mark each term as odd or even and describe what you notice about the sequence of colours.
Record each term in a table with two columns: term number (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and value, so emergent features line up next to their positions.
Predict whether the 10th term will be odd or even, then generate it and check.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule states a step, but the generated sequence can show a feature the rule never mentioned — here the terms strictly alternate odd, even, odd, even — and a table or parity colouring makes that feature visible.

activities.title: Explain WHY the feature must continue
feedback: If you say a feature 'just is' (e.g. 'the terms are all even because they just are'), push for the reason: even + even = even, so an even start plus an even step stays even.
If you predict odd terms will appear in 'start at 2, add 4', generate a few terms to test the prediction, then reason that adding an even step preserves evenness.
A correct explanation points to the step being odd or even (and, for an all-even or all-odd pattern, to the starting number's parity too) — not simply to the terms you happened to list.
activities.rationale: The objective's heart is informal explanation grounded in structure; pressing past restatement to a parity/digit reason is what distinguishes procedural term-cranking from the intended reasoning.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: For 'start at 1, add 3', explain why the odd/even labels keep alternating: adding 3 (an odd number) flips parity every single time, so the alternation must continue forever, not just for the terms you wrote.
For 'start at 2, add 4', predict before writing whether every term will be even, then justify: starting even and adding an even number keeps the result even, because even + even = even.
State a prediction for a step of 2 instead of 3 and explain how the parity pattern would differ (adding an even number leaves parity unchanged).
Give a structural reason, not just a restatement: say WHY it happens from the rule, not merely THAT it happens.
activities.intendedInsight: An emergent feature can be justified from the structure of the rule: an odd step makes the terms alternate (and the starting number fixes which parity the alternation begins with), while an even step keeps every term the same parity (and the start fixes that parity). So the feature must hold for all terms, not just the observed ones.

activities.title: Vary the step to discover the roles of start and step
feedback: If changing only the step also seems to change which parity the terms begin from, check that you really held the starting number fixed — change one thing at a time.

If you can't yet say why the colour locks for an even step, connect it back to the fact that adding an even number never changes parity (even + even = even, odd + even = odd), while adding an odd number flips parity.
activities.rationale: Changing one variable at a time (step, then start) lets learners experimentally separate the two ingredients of the rule and avoid confusing the term-to-term rule with the position-to-term rule.
learnerActions: Keep the start fixed and change the step from 3 (odd) to 4 (even); generate both sequences and compare the parity colouring — alternating for the odd step, locked for the even step.
Now keep the step fixed and change the starting number; notice which feature changes (which parity the terms begin with) and which stays the same (whether they alternate).

Articulate the two distinct roles you discovered: the step's parity decides whether the terms alternate (odd step) or stay a single fixed parity (even step); the start fixes which parity the sequence begins with — the one it stays on for an even step, or the one it starts the alternation with for an odd step.
Test a prediction before computing: for a new rule, say what the hidden feature will be and why, then generate terms to confirm.
activities.intendedInsight: The starting number and the step play different roles in an emergent feature; experimenting by changing one at a time isolates each role.

activities.title: Growing shape patterns and position-to-term
feedback: If you predict later stages only by drawing every one, try using the stage number and the per-step growth to jump ahead, then check by drawing.
If your described rule doesn't reproduce the next term, re-count one stage and recompute the change between stages (it may be constant, or it may itself grow in a pattern, as in square arrangements).
activities.rationale: Including growing shape patterns alongside number patterns connects the picture to the count and seeds nth-term reasoning, as recommended for this objective.
sourceClaims: T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: Continue a growing dot or tile pattern by predicting the next three terms and describing the rule in words.
Count the dots/tiles in each stage and record stage number next to the count in a two-column table.
Link the stage (term) number to its count, and predict a later stage's count, explaining how you used the position rather than drawing every stage.
Notice any hidden feature in the counts (e.g. always even, or a repeating units digit) and explain it from how the shape grows each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Growing shape patterns connect the term number to a count, seeding position-to-term (nth-term) thinking and giving a concrete picture of an emergent numeric feature.

activities.title: Pattern-detective discussion: justify the feature aloud
feedback: For 'would 30 ever appear from start 1, add 3?': the terms are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … and each one is one more than a multiple of 3 (it leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3). 30 is itself a multiple of 3 (remainder 0), so it can never appear. Notice that 30 is even and ends in 0 — and terms ending in 0, like 10, 40, 70, do occur — so parity and the units digit alone do NOT settle it; you have to reason from the step, that every term stays one more than a multiple of 3.

If your answer repeats the observation, the detective should ask 'but WHY will that keep happening?' until you name the structural cause — such as the step's parity, the even+even rule, or (for questions like whether 30 appears) the remainder every term leaves when divided by the step.
activities.rationale: A questioning dialogue that refuses restatement and demands a structural reason is well matched to the informal-explanation demand and pairs naturally with a generated sequence and table the learner has built.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a 'pattern detective', state a feature you noticed and be ready to defend it.
The detective accepts the feature ONLY when you give a structural reason for why it continues (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), not when you restate the observation.

Answer probing questions such as: 'Besides adding 3, what pattern do you see in the numbers?', 'Why do the terms of start-at-2-add-4 stay even?', 'If you start at 1 and add 3, would 30 ever appear — how can you tell?', and 'What changes if the step is 2 instead of 3?'
Revise your explanation if it's only a restatement until it names the structural cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining informally means giving a reason rooted in the rule's structure that shows a feature must persist, not merely reporting what you saw.

constraints: The aim is both skills together: generate accurately AND notice-then-explain a feature not stated by the rule; listing correct terms alone does not meet the objective.
Explanation must be structural (why the feature must continue), not a restatement of the observation.
Distinguish the term-to-term rule (the step) from a position-to-term rule; keep the starting number's role separate from the step's role.

Response formats that only ask a learner to pick the correct explanation from options can check whether they can distinguish a reason from a restatement, but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and voicing their own structural justification; use them to assess, and pair with tasks where the learner generates terms and explains in their own words.

A static exemplar table and growing-shape picture can anchor the idea and reveal a feature, but cannot let the learner vary the rule and test how emergent features change; provide that experimentation separately.

Interactive examples (auto-colouring terms by parity, a table filling in as terms are generated, a reveal-the-reason prompt, changing the step to compare) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tools.
Do not over-generalise a short-run observation; require justification before accepting that a feature always holds.

When judging whether a target value can appear in an arithmetic sequence, reason from the step's effect on remainders/divisibility, not from parity or units digit alone, since those surface features can be insufficient (e.g. 30 is even and ends in 0 yet cannot appear in 1, 4, 7, 10, …).

State the role of the step precisely: an odd step makes terms alternate in parity while an even step holds a single parity; the start only sets which parity begins the sequence, so avoid saying terms 'settle/lock to a value' in the alternating (odd-step) case.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'poor-fit' note claimed a third dimension 'adds no explanatory power'; this has been dropped as a catalog-preference statement rather than retained as a universal claim. Number/shape sequences are naturally represented in a table and growing picture, but no necessity claim is asserted.
Two of three cited sources were marked unverified in the source row (CCSS 4.OA.5 wording and NCETM guidance); treat their claims as legacy-stated, not independently re-checked here.

Self-audit of worked values: 'start 1, add 3' gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 (units digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2); 'start 2, add 4' gives all even terms; the '30' probe is determinate (terms ≡1 mod 3, 30 ≡0 mod 3, so 30 never appears). These were checked and are consistent.

Correction applied this pass: the 'Explain WHY' intendedInsight and the 'Vary the step' action/feedback said the start sets a 'value they lock to / settle on', which is false for the alternating odd-step case; reworded so locking is attributed only to even steps and the start is described as setting the starting parity. The sourceClaims on the 'Vary the step' activity were set to [] because no source claim directly supports the controlled-variation principle.

probeDeeper: Besides 'add 3', what pattern do you see in the numbers you wrote?
Why do the terms of 'start at 2, add 4' stay even every time?
If you started at 1 and added 3, would 30 ever appear? How can you tell?
What would change about the odd/even pattern if the step were 2 instead of 3?
assess.correctAnswer: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 — the child should notice a feature not in the rule, e.g. the terms alternate odd, even, odd, even, or the ones-digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2. For 'start at 2, add 4': all terms even, because starting even and adding an even number keeps it even. The teacher watches for correct generation AND an informal 'why' for a spotted feature.

errorPatterns.pattern: applies the rule inconsistently — adds the step to the wrong term, or changes the step partway
errorPatterns.nextMove: have the child mark the +3 jump between each pair on a number line so the constant step is enforced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: terms don't have a constant difference (e.g. 1,4,7,9,12)

errorPatterns.pattern: generates terms correctly but notices NO feature beyond the rule — just re-states 'it goes up by 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt attention to the ones-digits or odd/even alternation; model 'the rule says add 3, but look — the last digits go 1,4,7,0… why might that repeat?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked what else they notice, child only repeats the given rule

errorPatterns.pattern: spots a feature but cannot explain informally why it happens (e.g. sees all-even but says 'it just is')
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach pattern generation; scaffold the reason — even + even = even, so starting even and adding even stays even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct observation, no reasoning when asked why

errorPatterns.pattern: predicts wrongly that 'start at 2, add 4' will include odd numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: generate a few terms to check the prediction, then reason about why even+even stays even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child predicts odd terms will appear, not seeing that adding an even step preserves parity

responseLevels.gap: cannot generate a consistent pattern, or lists terms but notices/explains no feature.
responseLevels.full: generates the sequence accurately, identifies a feature not given by the rule, and explains informally why it must occur (parity/digit-cycle reasoning), transferring it to a new rule.
responseLevels.partial: generates terms correctly and spots a hidden feature but cannot explain informally why it occurs, or predicts parity incorrectly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rule and watch them generate and analyse the pattern: 'Start at 1 and keep adding 3 — write the first eight terms.' Then ask: 'What do you notice about the pattern that the rule didn't tell you?' Then give 'start at 2, add 4' and ask them to predict, before writing, whether all the terms will be even and why. Watch the term generation and the informal explanation of a hidden feature.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Generating terms is routine; the objective's heart is NOTICING a feature the rule didn't state and explaining WHY. Watching whether the child only lists terms versus spots-and-justifies a pattern (alternating parity, digit cycles) separates procedural term-cranking from the intended reasoning.
